# Cybersecurity Engineering Laboratories

Fourteen laboratories from the Cybersecurity Engineering course at Wrocław University of Science and
Technology, **carried out in 2022** and imported into git in 2026. The deliverable is written reports:
14 PDFs totalling exactly 182 pages, plus ~20 small input fixtures, 6 rendered screenshot pages and
one 50-line stdlib-only Python helper.

> "The course builds in one direction: understand a primitive, break it, then use what survives to
> defend a system."
> — Cybersecurity-Engineering-Laboratories/README.md, 2026-07-25

**Status: coursework, finished and frozen at last commit 2026-07-25.** The course is done and nothing
is maintained ("All finished and frozen" — interview, 2026-07-28). The `abandoned` tag on this page
refers to the individual exercises the reports themselves record as unfinished (below), not to the
repository.

## The arc

`labs/NN_topic/` numbered directories, 01 through 14, with the first two merged — the reading-order
variant of [[numbered-stages-in-directory-names]].

| Labs | Topic | Concept pages |
|---|---|---|
| 01–02 | Environment build; classical ciphers, entropy across six languages | [[cryptanalysis-by-measurement]] |
| 03 | Symmetric ciphers, stream and block, modes of operation | [[block-cipher-modes]] |
| 04–05 | RSA across key lengths; attacks on modern ciphers | [[symmetric-vs-asymmetric-cryptography]] · [[rsa-and-integer-factorization]] |
| 06–07 | Hashes, DSS, Diffie–Hellman; OpenSSL/PGP/PKI, CA build | [[digital-signatures]] · [[public-key-infrastructure]] |
| 08 | Network security — ARP poisoning and DNS spoofing | [[man-in-the-middle-attack]] |
| 09 | Secure communication — SSH, VPN, TLS, and their cost | [[cia-triad]] |
| 10–11 | Passive OSINT, then active enumeration | [[network-reconnaissance]] |
| 12 | Exploitation and reverse shells | [[metasploit]] · [[nmap]] |
| 13–14 | Web security tooling, then injection classes | [[web-application-injection]] · [[owasp-zap]] |

## Stack

[[cryptool]] 1 carries labs 01–06. [[openssl]] with GnuPG and Easy-RSA carries the applied-crypto
lab. [[wireshark]] captures in labs 08–09, with OpenVPN, SSH and netcat providing the transports.
[[nmap]] and [[metasploit]] carry recon and exploitation; [[owasp-zap]] and Burp Suite carry the web
labs against OWASP Juice Shop. Everything runs on VirtualBox VMs — [[kali-linux]] as the attack host,
Ubuntu Server, Metasploitable 2/3 and pfSense as targets.

**Balance: predominantly offensive.** Labs 02–06 are cryptanalysis and measurement; 08 and 10–14 are
attack. The defensive core is exactly two labs — 07 (PKI, CA, trust) and 09 (VPN/TLS/SSH plus capture
analysis).

## Findings

- **The reports are substantially more incomplete than the README implies.** The README calls the 182
  pages a record of "what was attempted, what the tools returned, and what the result means"; the
  reports themselves record repeated failures: the lab-06 Diffie–Hellman exchange over OpenSSL
  ("did not work", "not resolved"), the lab-12 exploitation chain ending in an empty directory, ZAP
  fuzzing in lab 13 ("it did not fuzz"), tooling install errors in labs 10 and 11, and two lab-02
  tasks marked "Did not do." Lab 01's report is effectively screenshots — roughly 400 characters of
  extractable text across 5 pages, and lab 12 is nearly the same. Two of the fourteen reports carry
  almost no prose at all. This is a clear instance of [[documentation-drift]]: the polished README
  overstates the completeness of what it indexes. `confidence: high` — read from the PDFs directly.
  That the failures are *recorded in place at all*, rather than quietly dropped, is the habit written
  up as [[lab-report-with-working-shown]] — the drift is in the summary, not in the reports.
- **Some theory answers are visibly filler.** Several question blocks are generic, one defers to what
  a "simple google search shows" (lab 09), and one openly credits an outside video (lab 08). The measured work (entropy tables, timing
  matrices, histogram comparison) is the strong part; the essay answers are not evidence of
  understanding and no concept page here cites them as such.
- **Key-material discipline is real and documented.** `.gitignore` excludes `*.p12`, `*.pem`, `*.key`,
  `*.jks` and `id_rsa*`; the README names the private-key screenshot it deliberately did not use; the
  fixtures are generated rather than committed. See [[omit-rsa-private-key-screenshot]] and
  [[generate-fixtures-not-commit]]. The strongest instance of
  [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]] in the source set after the Oracle repo.
- **Scope is stated in the repo, not inferred by the wiki.**

  > "This is coursework, carried out in 2022 against lab environments and deliberately vulnerable
  > targets provided for the purpose. ... Nothing here was run against a system without
  > authorisation, and none of it is written as an operational guide."
  > — Cybersecurity-Engineering-Laboratories/README.md, 2026-07-25

- **No polish tail.** README, `LICENSE` and `.gitignore` land together in the final commit `df046dc`;
  no badges, no separate license commit. Another **counter-example** to
  [[presentation-polish-tail-commits]], while the README remains a [[readme-as-guided-tour]].
- No `.gitattributes` and no Git LFS: 14 PDFs and 6 PNGs are committed as plain blobs.

## Redaction note — this repo is handled differently

The raw reports contain credentials captured in the MitM lab, ciphertext blocks, an identifier-derived
factorisation input, exploit-chain steps and injection payload strings. **None of it is reproduced
anywhere in this wiki.** Every concept page derived from this repo describes the technique class, what
it demonstrates and what defence it motivates — and stops there.

**The blanket `publish: false` was lifted on 2026-07-30; the redaction was not.** The two were doing
different jobs and the blanket was the weaker of them. Redaction is enforced by what the pages
*contain* — re-read on 2026-07-30 against payload strings, credentials, hashes, CVE identifiers,
target addresses and person-like values, and `audit-secrets` re-checks the published subset on every
build. The blanket was enforced by a flag, and its stated reason — keeping §9's "a public page may
not link a private one" from forcing a self-contained rewrite that would tempt detail back in — was
answered better elsewhere: the renderer emits an unpublished target as plain text, so no page has
ever needed rewriting to avoid a dead link.

What that leaves is the real line, and it is a line about content rather than about a cluster: **a
page here may name a technique class, a tool's behaviour and the defence it motivates. It may not
carry a payload, a captured credential, a target identifier or a working step of an exploit chain.**
Lab 12's chain is recorded as attempted and partly failed, with no step reproduced. That rule holds
whatever the publish flag says.
